plan.title: Corporate Video Production: A Practical Guide
plan.h1: Corporate video production: what to plan before you film
brief: What a business actually needs video for: a brand film, product demos, explainers, testimonials-style interviews with your own team, social cut-downs - and which one to make first.
Planning before filming: the one message, the audience, where it will play (website hero, social, ads, sales calls) and the lengths and ratios each place needs.
The production stages in plain words: script and storyboard, shoot, edit, motion graphics, sound, captions, delivery formats.
Getting more from one shoot: plan the vertical cut-downs, stills and website loops at the same time.
How video sits on a website without slowing it down (compressed loops, posters, lazy loading).

Visual design and a small design system: type, colour, components, states (empty, loading, error) and dark mode.
Prototypes and testing with real people before development starts.
Handoff to development and what changes for iOS, Android and web apps; App Store and Google Play details that affect design.

plan.title: Fixed Price vs Hourly Web Design: Which Wins?
plan.h1: Fixed price or hourly: how to pay for a website
keywords: how much does a website cost
brief: The three common models: fixed price for an agreed scope, hourly or day rate (time and materials), and retainers or monthly plans - how each works.
Who carries the risk in each: with fixed price the studio absorbs overruns inside the scope; with hourly the client does.
What a good fixed quote must spell out: pages and deliverables, revision rounds, what counts as a change, timeline, payment milestones, what happens after launch.
Where hourly genuinely fits better: open-ended discovery, ongoing improvements, work that cannot be scoped yet.
Red flags in either model. Be open that TheBrandle works at a fixed price (the homepage says so) and why, without turning the post into an advert.
For "how much does a website cost", link to the existing Dubai cost guide rather than repeating its price bands.

plan.title: SaaS Landing Page Design That Gets Sign-Ups
plan.h1: SaaS landing page design: what makes people sign up
brief: The structure of a landing page people act on: a headline that states the outcome, a real product visual, proof, how it works, benefits before features, pricing or the next step, objections answered, one call to action.
Choosing the conversion: free trial, demo, waitlist or contact - and what each asks of the visitor.
Forms: ask only for what the next step needs; every extra field has a cost.
Message match with ads and emails, page speed, and mobile layout as the default rather than an afterthought.
Measuring it: set up conversion events from day one, change one thing at a time, and judge on enough traffic.

plan.h1: A UI/UX design audit: how to find what is costing you users
brief: What a UX audit is and when a website or app needs one (falling sign-ups, support questions, a redesign coming).
The checks: navigation and labels, key journeys, forms, mobile use, accessibility basics, speed, consistency.
Using real evidence: analytics, recordings, support tickets and a handful of user tests.
Turning findings into a fix list ranked by effort and impact.
When an audit leads to small fixes and when it points to a redesign.

Editing and motion graphics that keep the brand consistent across every video.

plan.title: High-Converting Website Design: What Works
brief: What a conversion and a conversion rate are, and how to calculate it (conversions divided by visitors). Explain why benchmark rates vary so much by industry and traffic source - and do not quote any benchmark figure.
The factors that move it: a clear offer, speed, trust and proof, friction (form length, steps, surprise costs), mobile UX, visible calls to action, and accessibility.
How to find where a site is losing people: analytics funnels, heatmaps and session recordings, and watching five real users try one task.
Quick fixes versus when a redesign is the honest answer.

plan.title: Logo Design Process: How a Good Logo Is Made

brief: Starting with the business, not the logo: audience, competitors, personality, where the logo has to work.

The logo system: primary, secondary, icon, and the files a business should receive.
